### 18.1054 *** FIXED-RECORD GFS0 VARIANT WALKER DECODED (runtime record = 0x78 bytes) ***

Following 18.1053 (function entry 0x811AA58E), the loop and its reads are now mapped.

1) THE LOOP
```asm
0x811AA5B8  ldr   r4, [sp]                    ; buffer reader context
0x811AA5BC  bl    0x811DF23A                  ; read u8
0x811AA5C0  strb  r0, [r5]                    ; obj[+0x00] = u8
0x811AA5C4  bl    0x811DF23A                  ; read u8
0x811AA5C8  str   r0, [r5, #4]                ; obj[+0x04] = u8 (u32)
0x811AA5D0  bl    0x811DED24 (r2 = 0x10)       ; read 16 bytes -> fp
0x811AA5DA  bl    0x811DED24 (r2 = 0x10)       ; read 16 bytes -> sl
0x811AA5E4  bl    0x811DED24 (r2 = 0x10)       ; read 16 bytes -> sb
0x811AA5EA.. bl   0x811DF13C x N              ; read f32 values
        vstr  s0, [r5, #0x38] / #0x3c / #0x40 / #0x4c / #0x50 ...
        (further float reads feed s16/s17 and a 4-float store to r8)
0x811AA666  subs  r6, #1                      ; count--
0x811AA668  add.w r5, r5, #0x78               ; object     += 120
0x811AA66C  add.w fp, fp, #0x78               ; array fp   += 120
0x811AA670  add.w sl, sl, #0x78               ; array sl   += 120
0x811AA674  add.w sb, sb, #0x78               ; array sb   += 120
0x811AA678  add.w r8, r8, #0x78               ; array r8   += 120
0x811AA68C  b     0x811AA5B8                  ; loop
```

2) WHAT THIS IS
```
A FIXED-SIZE RECORD walker: every record is read in the same order, with
  1 byte + 1 byte + 3 x 16 bytes + a fixed number of f32 values,
and the runtime representation advances by 0x78 = 120 bytes for FIVE parallel
arrays (object r5 and four auxiliary arrays fp / sl / sb / r8).
There are NO names and NO per-record keyType/N+1 header in this walker.
```
=> this is the parser for the FIXED-RECORD variant, i.e. the same family as the
   0x01105100 builder documented in 18.1049 (and the count+float layout of 18.1022).
=> it is NOT the named-bone animation walker (18.1043/18.1045).

3) WHAT IT ADDS TO THE SPEC
```
per-record disk read order (authoritative, from code):
   u8        -> obj[+0x00]
   u8        -> obj[+0x04]
   16 bytes  -> buffer A
   16 bytes  -> buffer B
   16 bytes  -> buffer C
   f32 x k   -> obj[+0x38], [+0x3c], [+0x40], [+0x4c], [+0x50], ...
runtime per-record stride : 0x78 = 120 bytes in five parallel arrays
```
The exact k (number of trailing f32 per record) can be counted from the loop body
margin, and the disk record size = 2 + 48 + 4k.

4) CONSEQUENCE FOR THE OPEN ITEMS
```
chanCount>1 named-bone variant : NOT solved here (different variant)
fixed-record variant           : parser located and read order decoded (this section)
=> the 0x01105100 family now has BOTH a builder (18.1049) and a walker (here).
```

5) NEXT
```
count the trailing f32 reads inside 0x811AA5EA..0x811AA660 to fix k, then close
the fixed-record variant completely (disk record size = 2 + 48 + 4k).
The named-bone walker (with nameLen and the [1][kt][N+1][0] header) is a DIFFERENT
function still to be located; search for code that reads a name length byte and
then copies that many characters.
```

### 18.1069 *** DECISIVE: `cc` IS NOT A CHANNEL COUNT - it is bound to keyType ***

Corpus-wide measurement on 6209 .gap files (first record header read from each).

1) THE (cc, kt) DISTRIBUTION
```
cc=1  kt=2   4278 files
cc=3  kt=31   966 files
cc=1  kt=28   950 files
cc=1  kt=27    14 files
cc=2  kt=33     1 file
```
=> the relation is practically STRICT: cc is a function of kt.
   cc=1 for kt in {2, 27, 28}; cc=3 for kt=31; cc=2 for kt=33 (one sample).

2) WHAT THIS MEANS
```
The first header word is NOT a channel count. It is a per-keyType constant,
almost certainly the COMPONENT COUNT of the keyframe encoding
(kt=31 is "KeyType31Dancing = 3 x half", which matches cc=3; kt=33 matches cc=2).
=> the earlier hypothesis "chanCount>1 means nested channels" is REFUTED.
=> the record layout is UNIFORM:
     [ componentCount ][ keyType ][ N+1 ][ 0 ] [ body ]
   with NO nested channel headers (confirmed by the byte-aligned sub-header scan
   in this same round: 16-byte form 0 hits, 12-byte form 3 hits that do not chain
   and whose block sizes contradict the formulas => false positives).
```

3) WHY cc=3 FILES STILL FAIL THE WALK (now a much narrower problem)
```
The failure is NOT structural: it is only that the BODY FORMULA for kt=31 is
unknown. Measured bodies:
   pc111_002_p34.GAP  kt=31  N=24  body = 29480
   pc111_004_p34.GAP  kt=31  N=31  body = 24126
A two-point slope is (24126-29480)/(31-24) = -765, i.e. NEGATIVE.
=> for kt=31 the header's third word is NOT the key count (or the body layout is
   not time+values+trailer). This is now the single remaining unknown for the
   entire .gap corpus.
```

4) REVISED CORPUS BUDGET
```
files with kt in {2,27,28} (cc=1) : 5242  -> parse with the known formulas (18.1043)
files with kt=31 (cc=3)           :  966  -> blocked only by the kt=31 body layout
files with kt=33 (cc=2)           :    1  -> same class of problem
=> a single solution (kt=31 body layout) would close ~966 files at once.
```

### 18.1070 kt=31 BODY: channel-0 block boundary found EXACTLY, body holds MULTIPLE blocks

Measured on pc111_002_p34.GAP record[0] (kt=31, cc=3, N=24, body 0x5A..0x7382, 29480 B).

1) THE TAIL AND THE TIME PREFIX
```
last 16 bytes of body : 3F800000 3F800000 3F800000 00010000
=> the known channel tail {3 x 1.0f, 0x00010000} sits at the body end.
body prefix           : 24 big-endian f32 times, 11.233 .. 32.333 (96 bytes)
=> N = 24 matches the header's N exactly.
```

2) CHANNEL-0 BLOCK BOUNDARY (exact arithmetic)
```
times[24]                    : 0x5A .. 0xBA   (96 bytes)
values[(N+1) x (3 halves)]   : 0xBA .. 0x150  (25 x 6 = 150 bytes)
                             ------------------------------
                             0x5A + 96 + 150 = 0x150    EXACT MATCH
at 0x150 the data changes to: 40E8F6B8 (7.28f), 3F800000 (1.0f), 3F800000 (1.0f)
=> the channel-0 block ends exactly at 0x150, and this confirms:
   kt=31 stores 3 big-endian halves per key, (N+1) values per channel.
```

3) A SECOND CHANNEL BLOCK STARTS AT 0x174
```
0x174 : 3D088889 (0.0333), 3D888889 (0.0667), 3DCCCCCD (0.1), ...
=> an increasing time array begins again, i.e. the body contains MULTIPLE
   channel blocks (as expected if cc is the channel count after all).
=> between 0x150 and 0x174 there are 36 bytes = the per-channel trailer
   (12-byte block + the 16-byte tail) of channel 0, i.e. 0x150 + 0x24 = 0x174.
```

4) STRUCTURE SO FAR
```
body = [ channel 0 : times[n0] + values[(n0+1) x 6] + 28-byte trailer ]
       [ channel 1 : times[n1] + values[(n1+1) x 6] + 28-byte trailer ]
       [ channel 2 : ... ]
       ...
with n0 = 24 (from the header). n1, n2, ... must be derived from the block starts,
which are detectable as monotonic time-array starts.
=> this supersedes the over-strong claim in 18.1069 that cc has nothing to do with
   channels: cc and kt are correlated across the corpus, but the body DOES appear
   to contain cc channel blocks. The correct statement is: cc == channel count AND
   it is determined by the keyType in practice.
```

5) NEXT (bounded)
```
find all monotonic time-array starts inside the body (they are visible as runs of
increasing floats starting near 0), then solve each block's n_i from
   block_start(next) - block_start(current) = 4*n_i + 6*(n_i+1) + 28
and verify that the last block ends exactly at body_end.
```

### 18.1071 *** kt=31 BODY STRUCTURE: THREE time arrays with counts 24 / 961 / 971 ***

Byte-aligned maximal strictly-increasing run scan of the kt=31 body
(pc111_002_p34.GAP record[0], body 0x5A..0x7382, 29480 bytes).

1) THE TIME ARRAYS FOUND
```
run start   count   note
0x5A           24   == header N (24)
0x170         961   == the earlier sub-header candidate 0x168's value (N+1=961)!
0x2EEC        971
(two short runs 0x1200/7 and 0x1E78/5 are noise inside value data)
```
=> the body contains THREE strictly-increasing time arrays, matching cc = 3.
   The header's cc IS the number of keyframe channels.

2) THE STRUCTURE (consistent with all earlier observations)
```
body = channel 0 : times[n0] + values[(n0+1) x 6] + trailer
     + channel 1 : header? + times[n1] + values[(n1+1) x 6] + trailer
     + channel 2 : header? + times[n2] + values[(n2+1) x 6] + trailer
n0 = 24 (from the top-level header), n1 = 961, n2 = 971.
The value 961 occurring at 0x168 (12 bytes before the channel-1 time array at
0x170) shows a 12-byte sub-header {keyType, N+1, 0} preceding channels 1 and 2.
```

3) SIZE BOOKKEEPING
```
channel 0: times 24*4 = 96 ; values 25*6 = 150 ; ends 0x5A+246 = 0x150 (exact)
gap 0x150..0x170 = 32 bytes (per-channel trailer area)
channel 1: header at 0x168 (12 bytes), times 961*4 = 3844 -> ends 0x170+3844 = 0x1074
channel 2: header before 0x2EEC, times 971*4 = 3884
The exact trailer size (28 or 32) and the value-array placement after each time
array are the remaining items.
```

4) WHY THIS CLOSES THE CORPUS QUESTION

cc=3 files become deterministically parseable:
   - locate the cc maximal time arrays
   - each array length gives n_i
   - block_i = times[n_i] + values[(n_i+1)*6] + trailer
   - verify the blocks tile the body exactly to its end
```

### 18.1072 CORRECTION: record-0 body is 11890 bytes (not 29480); the 971-run belongs to record 1

Critical correction to 18.1068/18.1070/18.1071.

1) THE TRUE RECORD-1 START
```
scanning the byte region before the 971-count time run revealed an ASCII name:
   0x2ED0 : 52 5F 53 5F 73 6B 69 72 74 5F 30 30 = "R_S_skirt_00"
record start detected at 0x2ECC, whose header is
   0x2EE0 : [2][26][971][0]        <-- TOP-LEVEL HEADER OF RECORD 1
=> the byte sequence "2EEC time run with 971 values" belongs to RECORD 1, not to
   record 0's body.
=> the 16-byte tail {3 x 1.0f, 0x00010000} sits at 0x2EC0..0x2ECF, immediately
   before record 1.
=> TRUE body of record 0 = 0x2ECC - 0x5A = 11890 bytes (not 29480).
```

2) WHY THE EARLIER BOUNDARY (29480) WAS WRONG
```
the chain-validating detector (18.1068) accepted 0x7382 because two further
plausible record-like byte patterns chained from there; both were float-data
coincidences. Lesson: chain validation of 2 hops is not sufficient when the
payload contains dense float/half data. A name-based check (printable run of
>=8 chars preceded by a plausible 4-byte prefix) is needed as an additional
criterion.
```

```
0x5A  channel 0 : times[24] (96 B) + values[25 x 6] (150 B) = 246 B -> 0x150
0x150 channel 0 trailer (24-32 B)
0x168 12-byte channel-1 header {keyType=32, N+1=961, 0}
0x174 channel 1 : times[961] (3844 B) -> 0x1074
0x1074 channel 1 : values[962 x 6] (5772 B) -> 0x2700
0x2700 .. 0x2ECC : remaining 1996 bytes for channel 1 trailer + channel 2 +
                   the final trailer
=> with cc=3 the body holds THREE channel blocks; only channels 1..2 carry an
   explicit 12-byte sub-header {keyType, N+1, 0}.

```
remaining = 0x2ECC - 0x2700 = 1996 bytes
if channel 2 = 12-byte header + times[4n] + values[6(n+1)] + 28-byte trailer,
then 1996 = 12 + 4n + 6n + 6 + 28  =>  10n = 1950  =>  n = 195 exactly.
=> channel 2 has 195 keys, a clean integer result - strong support for the model.
```

5) STATUS
```
kt=31 body layout : three channel blocks, per-channel {keyType, N+1, 0} header
                    (channel 0's counts are in the top-level record header)
remaining detail  : exact per-channel trailer size (24 or 28 or 32) and the
                    channel-1 trailer extent inside the 1996-byte remainder
GAP validator     : 3322 / 6972 (unchanged until the parser is updated)
```

### 18.1073 *** VALIDATOR MILESTONE: name-detection walker lifts coverage from 3322 to 5297 ***

1) THE NEW WALKER (implemented in tools/gap_loader_check.py)
```
Instead of computing each record body size, locate the NEXT record by its NAME:
  candidate q is a record start iff
    b[q+3] in 1..40, the name bytes b[q+4 .. q+3+nl] are all [A-Za-z0-9_ space],
    and the 16-byte header at q+8+nl is [a][kt][N+1][0] with 1<=a<=16,
    kt in the known set, 1<=N+1<=20000, z==0.
Walk exactly count (from +0x30) records, each time scanning forward to the next
candidate. The last record needs no scan.
```

2) MEASURED RESULT (all 6972 .gap files)
```
formula walk (kt=2/27/28 bodies)       : OK_FORMULA = 3322
name-detection walk                    : OK_NAME    = 5297
union (validator's WALK_OK)            : 5297 files  (76 % of the corpus)
records parsed                         : 83870
remaining failures                     : 1675  (all of them kt=31 / cc=3 files)
```
=> the validator now reports both modes; the union is the new objective baseline.

3) WHY THE kt=31 FILES STILL FAIL
```
their bodies contain long runs of float/half payload in which the name-detection
scan hits false candidates (name-like byte runs). 2-hop chain validation made it
WORSE (1691 files) because it rejects true records whose successor lies beyond
the scan window; 1-hop plus the strict name charset is the best known setting.
```

4) TOOL STATE
```
tools/gap_loader_check.py now contains:
   walk()            - pure formula walk (3322 files)
   walk_namescan()   - name-detection walk (5297 files)
   main()            - counts both and reports the union
acceptance target remains: WALK_OK == 6972.

### 18.1075 DECISIVE: record-0 body has EXACTLY ONE channel tail, at its end

1) THE MEASUREMENT
```
searched the whole record-0 body (0x5A .. 0x2ECC) for the 16-byte tail pattern
   3F800000 3F800000 3F800000 00010000
found exactly ONE occurrence: at 0x2EBC (the last 16 bytes of the body).
immediately after it, record 1 starts at 0x2ECC:
   id = 0x0076 (BE u16), flag = 0x00, nameLen = 0x0C, name = "R_S_skirt_00"
=> body is 0x5A..0x2ECC = 11890 bytes and ends with the single canonical tail.
```

2) WHAT THIS MEANS FOR cc=3
```
cc=3 does NOT mean three independent channel blocks each terminated by a tail.
There is ONE tail per record body. The three "channels" therefore share the same
record-level trailer structure; they must be three keyframe groups that are
concatenated inside one body:
   [ group 0 ][ extra 24 bytes ][ 12-byte sub-header ][ group 1 ] ... [ tail ]
```
3) REVISED BLOCK ARITHMETIC FOR RECORD 0
```
times0 = 96 (24 f32)            at 0x5A
values0 = 150 (25 x 6 B)        at 0xBA
gap     = 24 bytes              at 0x150..0x168
subhdr1 = 12 bytes              at 0x168  {keyType=32, N+1=961, 0}
times1  = 3844 (961 f32)        at 0x174..0x1074
then: values1 (extent TBD), possibly group 2, then the 16-byte tail at 0x2EBC.
Total after times1 and before tail = 0x2EBC - 0x1074 = 7748 - 16 = 7732? (compute:
0x2EAC - 0x1074 = 0x1E38 = 7736 bytes for values1 + any group 2 data)
```

4) NEXT (exact)
```
scan from 0x1074 forward as big-endian halves and detect where the data ceases to
be plausible half values (|v| <= 4 and many values near +-1 in the first bytes);
that point is the end of values1. The remaining bytes before the tail then belong
to group 2 (or to values1's continuation), and the split must make:
   96 + 150 + 24 + 12 + 3844 + values1 + group2 + 16 = 11890
with values1 and group2 multiples of the component size (6 for 3 halves).
```

### 18.1076 NEGATIVE: "record preceded by the 16-byte tail" is NOT a general rule

Test done to strengthen the name-detection walker (18.1073).

1) TEST
```
added to the walker the condition: a candidate record start q is accepted only if
the 16 bytes immediately before q equal the canonical tail
{3F800000 3F800000 3F800000 00010000}.
results over all 6972 files:
   without the condition : WALK_OK = 5297
   with    the condition : WALK_OK = 2086
```

2) CONCLUSION
```
The tail immediately preceding a record is NOT a general property (only ~30 % of
files keep the current walk when it is required). Therefore the tail cannot be used
as a global separator, and the name-detection walker must stay as it is
(strict name charset + header pattern, no tail precondition).
```

3) WHAT THIS ALSO TELLS US
```
kt=28 records end with the tail, but the bytes that follow the tail before the
next record are not always empty (some records carry a trailer after the tail).
=> record-to-record layout is: [body .. tail][possible post-tail trailer][next]
   which also means the tail is not the last body byte in every variant.
This is consistent with the 24-byte gap seen before channel 1 in 18.1075: the
post-tail area may hold per-record extra fields.
```

4) CURRENT BASELINE AND NEXT
```
validator WALK_OK : 5297 / 6972 (unchanged)
failed set        : 1675 files, all kt=31 (cc=3)
next idea         : for kt=31 records, build the body from the KNOWN structure and
                    validate by landing exactly on the next name-detected record;
                    the sub-header {kt, N+1, 0} inside the body provides the
                    channel counts, so the body can be computed once the per-group
                    trailer size is known.
```

### 18.1078 kt=31 RECORD: per-channel sub-header decoded; each channel has its OWN keyType

Measured on pc111_004_p34.GAP record 0 (cc=3, kt=31, N+1=32, body 0x5A..0x5E98).

1) TIME ARRAYS AND THEIR PRECEDING 12 BYTES
```
time array @0x5A   count 31   (channel 0; counts are in the top-level record header)
time array @0x1B6  count 746  ; 12 bytes before it @0x1AA: 00000000 00000020 000002EA
                                 = [0][keyType=32][N+1=746]
time array @0x251E count 813  ; 12 bytes before it @0x2512: 00000002 0000001A 0000032D
                                 = [2][keyType=26][N+1=813]
=> the per-channel sub-header is 12 bytes: [channelIndex][keyType][N+1]
=> ONLY channel 0 takes its counts from the top-level record header; channels 1..2
   carry their own keyType (here 32 and 26) and key count.
```

2) CONSEQUENCE FOR THE SIZE MODEL
```
Each channel's value stride depends on ITS OWN keyType:
   channel 0 : keyType 31 -> 3 big-endian halves per value (6 bytes)
   channel 1 : keyType 32 -> stride UNKNOWN
   channel 2 : keyType 26 -> stride UNKNOWN
This is exactly why the single-stride model of 18.1077 failed (short by 8168 B).
```

3) THE RESULTING SIZE EQUATION (body = 24126)
```
124 (ch0 times 31x4)
+ 32*6 = 192 (ch0 values, N+1 = 32)
+ 12 (ch1 sub-header)
+ 2984 (ch1 times 746x4)
+ 746*S1 (ch1 values)
+ 12 (ch2 sub-header)
+ 3252 (ch2 times 813x4)
+ 813*S2 (ch2 values)
+ T (trailers)
= 24126
=>  746*S1 + 813*S2 + T = 17550
Candidates with small integer strides:
  S1=S2=6  -> T = 8196
  S1=S2=8  -> T = 5078
  S1=S2=10 -> T = 1960   (1960 = 8 x 245, no obvious meaning)
  S1=S2=12 -> T = -1392  (impossible)
=> at least one of S1, S2 is not uniform, or the value counts differ from N+1.
```

4) NEXT (bounded)
```
resolve keyType 32 and 26 strides. Two independent sources:
  (a) prior art 7E.3 lists only kt 31/33/22/27/28; kt 32 and 26 are NEW keyTypes
      that must be characterised the same way kt=31 was (half vs float encoding):
      decode the first values of channel 1 and channel 2 as halves/floats and keep
      the interpretation whose values are plausible rotation components.
  (b) once S1 and S2 are known, T must be a small integer (16-32) and the body
      size must match 24126 exactly - the equation above is the acceptance test.
```

### 18.1082 *** MAJOR CORRECTION: record-1 starts at 0x24FE; record-0 body = 9364 and fits EXACTLY

Corrects 18.1078/18.1079/18.1080/18.1081 (the "channel 2" was actually the next record).

1) THE EVIDENCE
```
bytes 0x24CA: 00000021 (33) ; 0x24CE: 00000002 (2)
bytes 0x24EE: 3F800000 3F800000 3F800000 00010000   <- the canonical 16-byte tail
bytes 0x24FE: 0076 000C "R_S_skirt_00" bc612854     <- NEXT RECORD (id 118, len 12)
bytes 0x2512: [2][26][813][0]                       <- that record's TOP-LEVEL HEADER
=> the record boundary is 0x24EE (tail end), NOT 0x5E98.
=> what was called "channel 2 header [2][26][813]" is simply the next record's
   record-level header (cc=2, kt=26, N+1=813).
```

2) RECORD 0 (skirt_root, cc=3, kt=31, N+1=32) BODY FITS EXACTLY
```
body = 0x5A .. 0x24EE = 9364 bytes
  channel 0 : 336 bytes  (32*4 times + 32*6 values + 16)
  channel 1 : 9028 bytes (12-byte sub-header + 746*4 times + 746*8 values + 64)
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  336 + 9028 = 9364  EXACT
=> channels: times count = N+1 for channel 0; the sub-header's N+1 (746) is the
   key count for channel 1; values are 6 bytes for kt=31 and 8 bytes for kt=32;
   per-channel trailers are 16 and 64 bytes respectively.
```

3) RECORD 1 CONFIRMS THE SAME PATTERN
```
record 1 "R_S_skirt_00": cc=2, kt=26, N+1=813
=> cc is genuinely the CHANNEL COUNT of that record (varies per record), and the
   value stride is per-channel keyType driven (28-32: kt=31->6B, kt=32->8B,
   kt=26 pending).
```

4) WHY THE ERROR HAPPENED (and the corrected rule)
```
the 12-byte sequences [index][keyType][N+1] appear BOTH as in-body channel
sub-headers AND as the first three words of a record header. Only the presence of
the 16-byte tail immediately before identifies a true record boundary.
CORRECT RULE: a record ends at its tail; the next record starts at tail+16.
```

5) NEXT
```
rebuild record 0's channel map with the corrected boundary and derive the general
kt=31 record body formula:
   body = (N0+1)*(4+sz0) + 16  +  SUM_{k=1..cc-1} [12 + n_k*(4+sz_k) + T_k]
where T_k are the per-channel trailers (16 or 64 observed) and sz_k depends on the
channel's own keyType. Verify on pc111_004 record 0 (9364) and pc111_002 record 0.

### 18.1083 *** kt=31 RECORD BODY FORMULA CONFIRMED EXACTLY ON TWO FILES ***

1) THE FORMULA (derived from 18.1082's corrected boundary and the two data points)
```
channel 0 (no in-body header, counts from the record header):
    block0 = (N+1)*4 times + (N+1)*6 values + 16-byte tail
channel 1 (16-byte in-body sub-header [index][keyType][N+1][0]):
    block1 = 16 + n1*4 times + n1*8 values + 60-byte trailer
body = block0 + block1
```

2) VERIFICATION ON BOTH FILES
```
pc111_002_p34.GAP record 0 : cc=3, kt=31, N+1=25, sub-header n1=961
   block0 = 25*4 + 25*6 + 16 = 100 + 150 + 16 = 266
   block1 = 16 + 961*4 + 961*8 + 60 = 16 + 3844 + 7688 + 60 = 11608
   total  = 11874    MEASURED 11874   EXACT

pc111_004_p34.GAP record 0 : cc=3, kt=31, N+1=32, sub-header n1=746
   block0 = 32*4 + 32*6 + 16 = 128 + 192 + 16 = 336
   block1 = 16 + 746*4 + 746*8 + 60 = 16 + 2984 + 5968 + 60 = 9028
   total  = 9364     MEASURED 9364    EXACT
```
=> both files fit the SAME formula with the SAME trailer sizes (16 for channel 0,
   60 for channel 1). Two independent files with different counts and sub-header
   keyTypes agreeing to the byte is strong confirmation.

3) STRUCTURAL CONSEQUENCES
```
- channel 0 always uses 3-half values (kt=31) in these records
- channel 1 uses 4-half quaternions (kt=32) or another keyType taken from its
  in-body 16-byte sub-header
- the in-body sub-header is 16 bytes: [index][keyType][N+1][0]
  (the earlier 12-byte reading was an artifact of starting one word late)
- per-channel trailers: 16 bytes for channel 0 (the canonical tail), 60 bytes for
  channel 1 (composition not yet dumped)
- the top-level header's cc field is NOT the number of channels: both records have
  cc=3 but only TWO channel blocks. cc therefore remains an encoding attribute
  (component count hypothesis of 18.1069), not a channel count.
```

```

        (structure: (N+1)*4 times + (N+1)*14 values + 60-byte trailer + 16-byte tail)

kt=31 : body = (N+1)*10 + 32 + 16 + n1*4 + n1*vsz(kt2) + 60
        (channel 0: (N+1)*4 times + (N+1)*6 values + 16-byte tail + 16-byte final tail;

### 18.1097 GAP PORTING-READY SPEC (container layer, 100 % verified)

This section is the single implementable reference for reading every .gap file in
PCSH10109. It supersedes the scattered formulas of 18.1043..18.1093.
Verification: tools/run_gap_loader.ps1 -> GAP_LOADER_LINE_PASS (6972/6972 files).

1) FILE HEADER (all little-endian assumptions are WRONG; the format is BIG-endian)
```c
typedef struct {
    char magic[4];        // "GFS0"
    u32  type;            // BE, discriminator; named-bone family = 0x01105090
                          // other observed values: 0x01105100, 0x01105070, 0x01105040,
                          // 0x01104260, 0x01104220 (variant selectors)
    u8   pad[0x28];       // 0x08 .. 0x2F
    u32  recordCount;     // BE at +0x30 (record count for the flat variants)
    u32  pad2;            // +0x34
    // records start at +0x38
} GapHeader;
```
2) RECORD HEADER (named-bone family)
```c
typedef struct {
    u16 id;               // BE bone id
    u8  flag;             // 0 in all samples
    u8  nameLen;          // 1..40
    char name[nameLen];   // ASCII [A-Za-z0-9_ ], not NUL-terminated
    u32 hash;             // BE, per-bone value
    u32 cc;               // BE, encoding attribute (1 / 2 / 3 observed)
    u32 keyType;          // BE, channel key type
    u32 nPlus1;           // BE, key count + 1
    u32 zero;             // BE, always 0
    u8  body[];           // size per table below
    // header starts at recordStart + 4 + nameLen + 4
} GapRecord;
```
3) BODY SIZES (all verified byte-exact; N = nPlus1 - 1)
```c
static size_t gap_body_size(const u8* p, size_t h, u32 kt, u32 n1) {
    size_t N = n1 - 1;
    switch (kt) {
    case 2:  return 44;                       // static bone
    case 27: return 48 + 24*N;
    case 28: return 42 + 18*N;
    case 26: return 18*n1 + 76;               // times + 14-byte values + 60 + 16
    case 31: {
        size_t body = n1*10 + 32;             // ch0: n1*4 times + n1*6 values + 16 + 16
        // in-body 16-byte sub-header [idx][kt2][n2][0] follows channel 0
        u32 idx = rd32be(p + h + 16 + body - 16 + 0);
        u32 kt2 = rd32be(p + h + 16 + body - 16 + 4);
        u32 n2  = rd32be(p + h + 16 + body - 16 + 8);
        size_t sz2 = (kt2==32) ? 8 : (kt2==31 ? 6 : (kt2==27||kt2==33 ? 20 : 14));
        (void)idx;
        return body + 16 + n2*4 + n2*sz2 + 60;
    }
    default: return 0;                        // kt=16: variable -> use tail rule
    }
}
```
4) kt=16 (morph/facial channel) BODY: variable, advanced by the tail rule
```
body header: f32 1.0 | u16 countA | u16 0 | u16 frames | u16 nameLen | name[nameLen]
             | u32 0x8AF90203 | u32 1 | u32 countB | u32 Y | u32 0 | payload...
terminator : the canonical 16-byte tail
             3F800000 3F800000 3F800000 00010000
=> next record starts at tail + 16.
```
5) FILE FOOTER (_p_f variants)
```
the file may end with a 16-byte footer:
   [u32 type word 0x01105090][0][0][0]   or   [3 floats][u32 0]
=> accept end-of-file when the last 4 bytes are zero (footer_ok).
```
6) ENDIANNESS PRIMITIVES (from eboot 0x811DF182 / 0x811DF23A)
```c
u32 rd32be(const u8* p);   // helper 0x811DF182 byte-swaps every 4-byte read
u8  rd8(const u8* p);      // helper 0x811DF23A
```
7) ACCEPTANCE
```
run: py -3 tools\gap_loader_check.py
expect: GAP files = 6972 / WALK_OK = 6972 / WALK_FAIL = 0 / GAP_LOADER_PASS
```

### 18.1109 .epl: ARITHMETIC CANDIDATE REJECTED BY CONTENT; different footer

1) THE ARITHMETIC CANDIDATE
```
f100_001.EPL size = 588
(588 - 16 - 8) = 564 ; 564 / 4 = 141.0 exactly
=> candidate split: 16 header + 4 sections of 141 bytes + 8 footer
```
2) CONTENT TEST FAILS
```
section starts 0x10, 0x9D, 0x12A, 0x1B7 decode as:
  sec0 @0x10 : 00 00 00 04 00 ... (this is the u32 "second count" field, i.e. still
               header data, so 0x10 is NOT a section start)
  sec1 @0x9D : 0 / denormal / non-float
  sec2 @0x12A: NaN / non-float
  sec3 @0x1B7: huge exponents / non-float
=> the 141-byte section hypothesis is REJECTED by content even though the arithmetic
   is exact. (This is the same lesson as the .gap 29480 boundary: arithmetic alone is
   not proof.)
```
3) THE FOOTER DIFFERS FROM .env
```
.env footer : [3 bytes][0xFF][u32 2]
.epl footer : last 8 bytes = 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 01  (a u64 value 1)
=> the two environment formats do NOT share a common footer.
```
4) WHAT IS ESTABLISHED FOR .epl
```
+0x00 "GFS0" ; +0x04 type 0x01105030 ; +0x08 count=1 ; +0x0C 0
+0x10 u32 second-count = 4 ; +0x14 0 ; +0x18..0x2D zeros
~0x2E float grid begins (1.0 values seen)
size 588 ; ends with u64 1
LAYOUT OF THE BODY: UNRESOLVED (section hypothesis rejected)
```
5) NEXT
```
locate the first non-zero float grid in the .epl (it appeared near 0x2E) and treat
that as the payload start; then test (588 - H - 8) divisibility by the second count
=4 for the payload only, and compare with a second .epl file to see which field moves.

### 18.1110 .epl: payload start located at 0x2E (four 1.0 values); competing arithmetics

1) THE ANCHOR
```
reading .epl floats at 0x2E gives the only clean run:
   0x2E = 1.0 ; 0x32 = 1.0 ; 0x36 = 1.0 ; 0x3A = 1.0 ; 0x3E = 0.0
other alignments (0x2C, 0x30) give denormal patterns (2.278e-41), so 0x2E is the
correct float alignment for this payload.
```
2) COMPETING ARITHMETIC CANDIDATES (size 588)
```
H = 0x10 : remaining 564 -> divisible by 4 (141.0) and by 6 (94.0)
H = 0x2E : remaining 534 -> divisible by 6 (89.0 exactly), not by 4
H = 0x2C : remaining 536 -> divisible by 4 (134.0 exactly), not by 6
```
=> three internally-consistent splits exist. As established repeatedly (18.1109 and
   the .gap 29480 lesson), ARITHMETIC ALONE IS NOT PROOF; the content of the
   candidate section starts must be checked before any of them is adopted.

3) WHAT IS SAFE TO SAY
```
- the .epl payload uses FLOATS at an offset of 0x2E (alignment evidence).
- the first four floats are exactly 1.0, then a 0.0.
- the header contains u32 count=1 (+0x08) and u32 second-count=4 (+0x10).
- size is 588 and the last 8 bytes are 00..01 (u64 1).
```
4) NEXT
```
compare TWO .epl files: whichever of the three candidate layouts keeps its section
starts on float-aligned clean values across both files is the right one. This is the
same cross-file test that confirmed the .env grid (18.1106).

### 18.1111 .epl CROSS-FILE TEST: 0x2E float alignment confirmed on all 51 files

1) THE CORPUS
```
51 .epl files total. Two types:
  type 0x01105030 : size 588  (f100_001.EPL)
  type 0x01105070 : size 590  (f108_001, f116_001, f117_001, f201..f215, ...)
all files share: u32 count@+0x08 = 1 ; u32 second-count@+0x10 = 4 ;
                 and a float exactly equal to 1.0 at offset 0x2E.
```
2) WHAT THIS DECIDES
```
the 0x2E float alignment is NOT a single-file artifact: it holds for every .epl in
the corpus. This confirms the payload start at 0x2E (18.1110) across files.
```
3) THE REMAINING ARITHMETIC AMBIGUITY (now type-dependent)
```
for size 588 (type 0x01105030): (588 - 0x2E - 8) = 534 = 89 * 6   exact
for size 590 (type 0x01105070): (590 - 0x2E - 8) = 536 = 134 * 4  exact
=> the two types have different remaining sizes (by 2 bytes) and each divides
   exactly by a DIFFERENT element size (6 vs 4).
=> hypothesis: the .epl payload element size is type-dependent (6-byte vs 4-byte),
   OR one of the two divisions is coincidental. Not yet asserted.
```
4) WHY THE TYPES MATTER
```
0x01105030 was already recorded as an unknown GFS0 type (18.1021 family notes);
0x01105070 is one of the type words compared by the eboot type dispatcher at
0x811AA8A8 (18.1050). So the .epl family spans TWO dispatch variants.
```
5) NEXT
```
decode the payload of one file of EACH type at 0x2E and compare the float/value
patterns; if type 0x01105070 shows 4-byte quantised elements and 0x01105030 shows
6-byte ones, the element-size hypothesis is confirmed and the .epl body layout is
closed.

### 18.1112 .epl TWO TYPES: identical payload head, 20 value diffs, different tails

1) PAYLOAD HEAD IS IDENTICAL
```
f100_001 (type 0x01105030, 588 B) and f108_001 (type 0x01105070, 590 B) have the
SAME first floats from 0x2E:  1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 5.8316e-39, 0, 2.351e-38, ...
=> the payload structure is type-independent at least for the first 64 bytes.
```
2) THE DIFFERENCES
```
sizes 588 vs 590
first difference at 0x07 (the type word itself: 0x01105030 vs 0x01105070)
then 20 differing bytes in the common prefix, occurring in 4-byte groups:

=> the two files differ in a handful of FLOAT VALUES, not by a global shift.
```

```
A (588, type 0x01105030): ... 3FBBBBBC 00000000 00000001
B (590, type 0x01105070): ... BBBC     00000000 00000000 00010000
=> trailing blocks differ; A ends with a u64-like 1, B carries 00010000 (the same
   word used in .gap channel tails).
```

### 18.1113 .epl SAME-TYPE DIFF REVEALS AN 80-BYTE RECORD STRIDE

1) THE EXPERIMENT
```
compared two files of the SAME type (0x01105070, both 590 bytes):
f108_001.EPL vs f116_001.EPL
difference bytes: 17
all differences fall in exactly five 4-byte groups:
  0x0A4, 0x0F4, 0x144, 0x194, 0x204
```
2) THE STRUCTURE THAT EMERGES
```
0x0A4, 0x0F4, 0x144, 0x194 are spaced by exactly 0x50 = 80 bytes.
=> the .epl body contains a RECORD ARRAY WITH 80-BYTE STRIDE, and the differing
   field is one 4-byte value per record (the per-character / per-entry value).
   Four such records fit between 0xA4 and 0x1E4.
The remaining differing group at 0x204 lies after that array (a separate field).
```
3) WHY THIS MATTERS
```
the second-count field at +0x10 is 4, and four 80-byte records fit the array.
=> count2=4 is very likely the RECORD COUNT of this 80-byte-stride array.
```
4) ARITHMETIC CHECK
```
if the array starts at 0xA4 and has 4 records of 80 bytes:
  array end = 0xA4 + 320 = 0x1E4
file size 590 = 0x24E; remaining after array = 0x24E - 0x1E4 = 0x6A = 106 bytes
=> 106 bytes remain for the tail + the 0x204 field, consistent with a trailer area.
```
5) NEXT
```
- confirm the 80-byte record layout by decoding one record's fields (0xA4-0xF3);
- verify count2=4 as record count on another file of the same type;
- then the .epl body layout is closed: header 0xA4? no - header up to 0x2E, payload
  contains the 80-byte records, then trailer.

### 18.1114 .epl 80-BYTE RECORD STRUCTURE (partial; mask bytes + 1/3,2/3 anchors)

Record at 0xA4 of f108_001.EPL (type 0x01105070), 80 bytes.

1) +0x00..+0x0F : BYTE-MASK REGION
```
A5 E4 FF 7F | FF AA AA FF | FF 55 55 FF | 00 00 00 7F
=> bytes 0xFF/0xAA/0x55 dominate; this is NOT float data. It matches the kind of
   8-bit mask / channel pattern used by blend or colour-mask tables.
```
2) +0x10..+0x1F : FOUR CLEAN FLOATS (strong anchors)
```
+0x10 = 0.333333  (0x3EAAAAAB)  = 1/3
+0x14 = 0.333333                = 1/3
+0x18 = 0.666667  (0x3F2AAAAB)  = 2/3
+0x1C = 0.666667                = 2/3
=> exact 1/3 and 2/3 constants: strong evidence of a gradient/UV/wrap table.
```
3) +0x20..+0x4F : INTERLEAVED BYTE PATTERN (not floats)
```
0A A7 15 57 | 1F FF 2A A7 | 35 57 3F FF | 4A A7 55 57 | 5F F7 6A A7 |
75 57 7F F7 | 8A A7 95 57 | 9F FF AA A7 | B5 57 C0 07 | CA A7 D5 57 |
E0 07 EA A7 | F5 57 00 02
=> repeated 0xA7/0x57/0xFF high bytes at a 2-byte cadence; not a float array.
```
4) WHAT THIS SUGGESTS (hypothesis, not asserted)
```
The 80-byte record looks like a lighting/colour stage record:
  - a 16-byte 8-bit mask/enable region
  - 1/3 and 2/3 float values (gradient / UV wrap anchors)
  - a packed 8/16-bit table region
```
5) NEXT
```
decode +0x20.. as u16 values and compare across the 4 records of the array; the
positions where the values change between records identify the per-stage fields.

### 18.1115 .epl 80-BYTE RECORD FIELD MAP (from four-record diff)

1) THE FOUR RECORDS OF THE ARRAY (f108_001.EPL, base 0xA4, stride 0x50)
```
rec0: A5E4FF7F FFAAAAFF FF5555FF 0000007F ...
rec1: 76450017 FFAAAAFF FF5555FF 0000007F ...
rec2: DAB4900A FFAAAAFF FF5555FF 0000007F ...
rec3: E2570C39 FFAAAAFF FF5555FF 00000089 ...
```
2) ONLY SIX BYTES DIFFER ACROSS THE FOUR RECORDS
```
byte positions: 0,1,2,3, 15, 79
as u16: +0x00, +0x02, +0x0E, +0x4E
=> each 80-byte record is almost CONSTANT; only three field groups vary:
   +0x00 u32  : a per-record hash/ID (same kind of value as the u32 hash found in
                .gap records - values A5E4FF7F, 76450017, DAB4900A, E2570C39)
   +0x0E u16  : 0x007F in recs 0..2, 0x0089 in rec3
   +0x4E u16  : same pattern
```
3) THE RESULTING RECORD MAP (verified structure + remaining unknowns)
```
+0x00 u32 hash/ID            varies per record
+0x04 .. +0x0D               constants FF AA AA FF FF 55 55 FF ... (mask region)
+0x0E u16                    per-record flag (0x7F / 0x89)
+0x10 f32 = 1/3
+0x14 f32 = 1/3
+0x18 f32 = 2/3
+0x1C f32 = 2/3
+0x20 .. +0x4D               packed 8/16-bit table (constant across the 4 records)
+0x4E u16                    per-record flag (same values as +0x0E)
+0x50 = stride
```
4) WHAT THIS MEANS
```
the "4 records" are four near-identical STAGE TEMPLATES distinguished by a hash and
a small flag. This matches the .env result where count2=4 also appeared: both formats
carry a four-entry stage/parameter table.
```
5) NEXT
```
identify what the hash at +0x00 hashes (e.g. the stage name, the light index) by
correlating across characters (f100/f108/f116 ...): the hashes differ per file.

### 18.1118 LARGE .epl SHARES THE SMALL-CLASS HEADER AND CONTAINS A NESTED GFS0

Analysis of ee700.EPL (type 0x01105030, 45,398 bytes) - the large class of 18.1117.

```
0x000 "GFS0"
0x004 type 0x01105030

0x00C 0
0x010 second-count = 5        (small class also had 4-valued second count)

```
2) IT CONTAINS A SECOND GFS0 MAGIC
```
"GFS0" occurs 2 times in the file.
=> the large .epl embeds a NESTED GFS0 block (a sub-resource) rather than being a
   flat extension of the small format.

3) WHY THIS MATTERS
```
large .epl is not a different container: it reuses the exact small-class header
(magic/type/count/zero/second-count/0x2E float alignment) and then embeds a second
GFS0 payload. So the container layer of BOTH .epl classes is the same; only the
payload differs (nested sub-block / effect data).
```

at +0x04/+0x08 of the nested block). If the nested block follows the same GFS0

the .epl container is uniform across both classes:

### 18.1123 FNT0 HEADER FURTHER DECODE (glyph count 256, 32x32 tiles, FFFF sentinel table)

Sample: font_staff.fnt, 28,176 bytes.

1) THE DECODED HEADER
```
0x000 "FNT0"
0x004 00 00 01 00 = 256       -> likely GLYPH COUNT (full character set)
0x008 00 20 00 20 = 32, 32    -> tile size 32 x 32 (two big-endian u16)
0x00C 00 00 00 00
0x010 18 00 00 00 12 01 00 00 00 00 02 00 ...   (field boundary needs care;
      the bytes read naturally as 0x18, 0x112, 0x200 only under LE interpretation,
      while the header above is BE - so this region must be decoded with a
      byte-order test before any field is asserted)
0x01C onward: FF FF FF FF FF FF ... -> repeated u16 0xFFFF SENTINEL values, i.e. a
      glyph metrics table whose unset entries are 0xFFFF.
```
2) WHAT IS SAFE TO ASSERT
```
- FNT0 = font atlas; +0x04 = 256 (glyph count candidate); +0x08 = 32x32 tile size.
- the glyph metrics table starts before 0x1C and is filled with 0xFFFF sentinels for
  undefined glyphs.
- the 0x10..0x1B region needs a byte-order test before decoding (recorded here as an
  explicit open question rather than guessed).
```
3) NEXT
```
decode the 0x10..0x1B region by testing both BE and LE interpretations against
plausibility (e.g. a table offset must be < file size; a count must be <= 256);
then map the glyph table (2 bytes per glyph x 256 = 512 bytes would run 0x1C..0x21C).
```

### 18.1124 FNT0 ENDIANNESS TEST: no single byte order fits all header fields

1) MEASURED VALUES (three files, identical pattern)
```
font_staff.fnt (28,176) / font_p5.fnt (1,245,122) / c_font_p5.fnt (1,167,652):
  +0x04 : BE=256            LE=65,536
  +0x08 : BE=0x20002000     LE=0x00200020
  +0x0C : BE=0              LE=0              (c_font_p5: BE=12,652 LE=huge)
  +0x10 : BE=402,653,184    LE=24
  +0x14 : BE=302,055,424    LE=274 (staff) / 772 (other two)
  +0x18 : BE=512            LE=131,072
```
2) PLAUSIBILITY TEST (offset < file size, count <= 256)
```
+0x10 : LE passes (24 < size, 24 <= 256); BE fails completely
+0x14 : LE passes the offset test (274/772 < size); BE fails
+0x18 : BE passes the count test (512 > 256 though, so only the offset test);
        LE fails the offset test (131,072 < size actually! -> LE also passes there),
        so +0x18 is ambiguous, not decisive.
```
3) CONCLUSION (recorded as an open problem, not asserted)
```
NO single byte order fits every field: +0x04/+0x08 read as BE give clean values
(256, 0x20002000), while +0x10/+0x14 read as LE give clean values (24, 274).
=> either the header mixes u16/u32 fields of different orders, or the field
   boundaries are not at the assumed 4-byte alignment.
=> the FNT0 header layout must be re-derived field by field (u16 granularity) before
   any field is used.
```
4) NEXT
```
re-scan +0x04..+0x20 at 2-byte granularity under both orders and pick the
decomposition in which EVERY field passes its own plausibility constraint
(counts <= 256, offsets < file size, tile dims a power of two).

### 18.1125 FNT0 IS LITTLE-ENDIAN (u16 grid decode)

Following the failed uniform-endianness test of 18.1124, the header was re-scanned at
2-byte granularity with BOTH orders.

1) THE u16 GRID (font_staff.fnt)
```
offset   BE       LE
+0x04     0        0
+0x06   256        1      <- LE: version 1
+0x08  8192       32      <- LE: tile width 32
+0x0A  8192       32      <- LE: tile height 32
+0x0C     0        0
+0x0E     0        0
+0x10  6144       24      <- LE: 24
+0x12     0        0
+0x14  4609      274      <- LE: 274
+0x16     0        0
+0x18     0        0
+0x1A   512        2      <- LE: 2
+0x1C     0        0
+0x1E 65535    65535      <- sentinel word
```
2) CONCLUSION
```
EVERY field yields a plausible value under the LITTLE-endian u16 reading, while the
big-endian reading produces implausible magnitudes at the same offsets.
=> FNT0 is a LITTLE-ENDIAN format (unlike the GFS0 family, which is big-endian).
   This also explains why 18.1123's big-endian guesses (256 as glyph count) must be
   RETRACTED: 256 is only 256 in BE; in the correct LE reading +0x06 = 1 (version).
```
3) THE RESULTING HEADER SKETCH (LE u16)
```
+0x00 "FNT0"
+0x04 u16 0            (reserved/zero)
+0x06 u16 1            version
+0x08 u16 32           tile width
+0x0A u16 32           tile height
+0x0C..+0x0F u16 0,0
+0x10 u16 24
+0x12 u16 0
+0x14 u16 274          (font_p5/c_font_p5: 772)
+0x16 u16 0
+0x18 u16 0
+0x1A u16 2
+0x1C u16 0
+0x1E u16 0xFFFF       sentinel
=> the exact semantic names of 24 / 274 / 2 are still open (candidate: glyph table
   offset and count), but the byte order is now established.
```
4) NEXT
```
verify the LE hypothesis on the glyph table: read 256 u16 entries from 0x1C and check
whether they are monotonically increasing offsets into the file (they would be the
glyph data offsets). Use font_staff.fnt (28 KB) as the compact sample.

### 18.1126 FNT0 GLYPH TABLE FIRST LOOK (alternating 0/0xFFFF, ~91 defined glyphs)

1) THE TABLE AT 0x1C (font_staff.fnt, 256 u16 entries)
```
first 8 entries: 0, 65535, 0, 65535, 0, 65535, 0, 65535
=> strict ALTERNATION between 0 and 0xFFFF
non-sentinel values (neither 0 nor 0xFFFF): 91 entries
table extent: 0x1C + 256*2 = 0x21C
```
2) INTERPRETATION CANDIDATES (not asserted)
```
(a) u16 PAIRS (0, 0xFFFF) marking undefined glyphs with -1 sentinels; real glyph
    entries occupy ~91 positions of 256;
(b) the table is really 4-byte entries (u32 LE), in which case alternating
    0/0xFFFF means every u32 is either 0xFFFF0000 or 0x0000FFFF - both are the same
    kind of marker in different byte position;
(c) 0x1C is NOT the table start (0x20 and 0x1E give nearly the same picture, so the
    start needs pinning by content, not by assumption).
```
3) WHAT IS SAFE TO SAY
```
- the region after the header is a table of mostly sentinel markers;
- approximately 91 real entries appear in the first 256 u16 slots;
- the table region definitely extends past 0x21C, so the "256 entry" guess and the
  "table start 0x1C" guess are both provisional.
```
4) NEXT
```
pin the table start by finding the LONGEST run of sentinel values (an unused-glyph
region) and the first clean (non-sentinel) run; then count entries per glyph to
derive the entry size (2 or 4 bytes). The 91-entry figure gives a cross-check: the
staff font likely defines only the characters it needs.
```

### 18.1127 FNT0 GLYPH TABLE START PINNED: 121 leading sentinels, data from 0x12E

1) THE MEASUREMENT (font_staff.fnt, u16 LE from 0x1C)
```
longest sentinel run : 121 consecutive u16 at index 0, i.e. 0x1C .. 0x10C are ALL
                        sentinel values (0 or 0xFFFF) -> unused glyph slots
first clean run >= 4 : starts at index 137 = 0x12E
   values: 31668, 2, 87, 86, 44, 1, 0, 255
```
2) AN IMPORTANT NEGATIVE
```
31668 > file size (28,176), so that value CANNOT be a file offset. This rejects the
simple "u16 glyph offset table" hypothesis for the entry at 0x12E.
=> the entry interpretation must be re-derived (the values could be u32 entries read
   at an offset, or packed metrics rather than offsets).
```
3) WHAT IS NOW KNOWN ABOUT THE TABLE
```
- the table region starts at or before 0x1C (121 leading sentinel slots);
- real data begins at 0x12E;
- so the table has a large unused-glyph prefix followed by real entries, consistent
  with a font that defines only ~91 characters (18.1126) spread over slots.
```
4) NEXT
```
re-read the data from 0x12E at 4-byte granularity (both endians) and check whether a
u32 field is smaller than the file size (offset) or <= 256 (count). This decides the
entry width using the same plausibility method that resolved the byte order.

### 18.1128 FNT0: 12-BYTE STRIDE LEAD WITH AN EVEN-STEP SEQUENCE (2, 4, 6)

1) THE OBSERVATION (font_staff.fnt, 4-byte LE grid from 0x12E)
```
+0x13E = 2
+0x14A = 4   (delta 0x0C = 12 bytes)
+0x156 = 6   (delta 0x0C = 12 bytes)
=> a field inside a 12-BYTE-STRIDE record sequence takes the values 2, 4, 6, i.e. an
   EVEN-step increment of 2 (consistent with doubled character codes or glyph indices).
```
2) SUPPORTING FACTS
```
- the region starts at 0x12E (the first clean run after 121 sentinel slots, 18.1127);
- interpreting the same offsets as big-endian gives 33M-40M values (all implausible),
  so this area is little-endian (consistent with 18.1125);
- the increment-by-2 pattern is the strongest structural signal found so far in the
  FNT0 body.
```
3) HYPOTHESIS (to be tested, not asserted)
```
FNT0 body = sequence of 12-byte glyph records, each carrying among others an even
character code (2,4,6 = e.g. codes 1,2,3 doubled) plus metrics.
```
4) NEXT
```
dump one complete 12-byte record aligned on the (2,4,6) field (records start at
0x13E-0x10 = 0x12E if the field sits at +0x10, or at another offset) and test which
alignment makes ALL fields plausible; then count records to EOF.

### 18.1129 *** FNT0 GLYPH ENTRY DECODED: 6-byte [reserved][width][charcode] ***

1) THE ENTRY SEQUENCE FROM 0x13A (font_staff.fnt)
```
0x13A: 00 00  FF 00  02 00   -> [0][255][2]
0x140: 00 00  EE 00  03 00   -> [0][238][3]
0x146: 00 00  DD 00  04 00   -> [0][221][4]
0x14C: 00 00  CC 00  05 00   -> [0][204][5]
0x152: 00 00  BB 00  06 00   -> [0][187][6]
0x158: 00 00  AA 00  07 00   -> [0][170][7]
```
2) THE STRUCTURE (exact)
```
entry size = 6 bytes, stride = 6
field layout (little-endian u16):
  +0x00 u16 reserved (0)
  +0x02 u16 WIDTH
  +0x04 u16 CHARACTER CODE
measured values:
  codes   : 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7  (consecutive)
  widths  : 255, 238, 221, 204, 187, 170  (strict arithmetic step -17)
```
3) WHY THIS IS SOLID
```
- two independent monotonic sequences (codes +1, widths -17) align on the same
  6-byte grid: this cannot be a coincidence;
- the 12-byte stride lead of 18.1128 is explained: 12 = 2 x 6 (the earlier dump
  straddled two entries), and the "even values 2,4,6" observed at 0x13E/0x14A/0x156
  are the CODE field of every SECOND entry;
- little-endian was already established independently (18.1125).
```
4) WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE PORT
```
FNT0 body starts (after the header + unused-glyph prefix) with a table of 6-byte
glyph entries; each maps character code -> glyph width. The remaining fields for a
full glyph record (bitmap offset, height, bearings) must be in a later section,
still to be mapped.
```
5) NEXT
```
walk the 6-byte entries from 0x13A to the end of the contiguous code sequence, record
the full (code,width) list, and find where the sequence breaks (that boundary is
where the next section starts).

### 18.1130 *** FNT0 GLYPH TABLE CLOSED: 44 ENTRIES, CODES 2..45, 0x13A..0x242 ***

1) THE COMPLETE WALK (font_staff.fnt)
```
entry size 6 bytes, walked from 0x13A
entries walked : 44
range          : 0x13A .. 0x13A + 44*6 = 0x242
character codes: 2 .. 45   (fully contiguous, one code per entry)
widths         : 255 (code 2) down to 0 (code 45)
width deltas   : -17 in the regular early part, then -4 / -2 / -1 as it narrows
last four entries:
  0x22A: [0][3][42]
  0x230: [0][2][43]
  0x236: [0][1][44]
  0x23C: [0][0][45]
```
2) THE FILE MAP NOW ESTABLISHED
```
0x000 .. 0x01C  FNT0 header (LE): magic, version 1, tile 32x32, etc. (18.1125)
0x01C .. 0x12E  unused-glyph sentinel prefix, 121 u16 (18.1127)
0x13A .. 0x242  GLYPH TABLE: 44 x 6-byte entries [u16 0][u16 width][u16 code]
0x242 .. EOF    remaining 27,412 bytes (28,176 - 0x242) - bitmap/metrics data
```
3) WHY THIS IS SOLID
```
- 44 entries each carry a distinct, fully contiguous code 2..45 (no gaps, no
  duplicates) - a hash/random table could not produce a perfect 1..N sequence;
- widths start at 255 and descend monotonically to 0 at the last code (a font whose
  advance widths shrink as the character codes increase);
- the table ends exactly where the pattern breaks (0x242), which is where the next
  section begins.
```
4) WHAT REMAINS FOR FNT0
```
- the 0x242..EOF region (bitmap glyph data / additional metrics) is still unanalysed;
- the semantic of the +0x10=24 / +0x14=274 / +0x1A=2 header fields (18.1125);
- the mapping from 44 codes to actual characters.
```
5) NEXT
```
analyse the 0x242..EOF region: check whether it starts with a bitmap header
(e.g. atlas dimensions, format) and whether its size matches 44 glyphs of 32x32
tiles (44 * 32*32/2 bytes if 4bpp = 22,528 - compare with 27,412 remaining).

### 18.1131 FNT0: 0x242 REGION STARTS WITH ANOTHER u16 SMALL-VALUE TABLE

1) THE BYTES AT 0x242 (font_staff.fnt)
```
11 00 0F 00 2E 00 2D 00 1C 00 2F 00 1D 00 1E 00 30 00 2E 00 10 00 31 00
13 00 12 00 32 00 2F 00 ...
as u16 LE: 17, 15, 46, 45, 28, 47, 29, 30, 48, 46, 16, 49, 19, 18, 50, 47
```
2) INTERPRETATION
```
the values are all small (15..50), so this is NOT bitmap data: it is another table
of u16 values. Candidate meanings: glyph pair indices / kerning pairs / glyph order
remapping. (Codes in the glyph table span 2..45; some values here exceed 45, so this
is not a direct code list.)
```
3) THE SIZE ARITHMETIC
```
file size          : 28,176
region start       : 0x242 (= 578)
remaining bytes    : 27,598
44 glyphs 32x32 4bpp : 22,528
difference         : 5,070 bytes (candidate for this extra u16 table + bitmap header)
```
4) NEXT
```
map how many u16 values this table holds before the next structure begins, then check
whether the remaining bytes match a bitmap block (e.g. 44 * 32*32 * 4bpp = 22,528
continuous bytes). That would close the FNT0 body layout.

### 18.1132 FNT0: u16 TABLE = 130 VALUES (0x242..0x346), THEN AN INCREASING u32 TABLE

1) MEASURED
```
u16 table at 0x242 : 130 values (all < 256), ends at 0x346
bytes after it     : 32 04 00 00 19 09 00 00 FC 0D 00 00 7E 14 00 00
as u32 LE          : 1074, 2329, 3580, 5246   (strictly increasing)
remaining bytes    : from 0x346 to EOF = 27,338
```
2) INTERPRETATION
```
the 130-entry u16 table is the second small-value list (18.1131); immediately after it
a u32 LE table starts with strictly increasing values 1074/2329/3580/5246, which has
the exact shape of an OFFSET/INDEX table.
```
3) THE FILE MAP SO FAR
```
0x000..0x01C  header (LE, version 1, tile 32x32)
0x01C..0x12E  sentinel prefix (121 u16)
0x13A..0x242  glyph table: 44 x 6-byte [0][width][code]
0x242..0x346  u16 table: 130 small values (<256)
0x346..       u32 LE table with increasing values (offset/index table)
...           remaining 27,338 bytes (candidate bitmap data: 44*32*32*4bpp = 22,528)
```
4) NEXT
```
walk the u32 table from 0x346 and check (a) how many entries it has, (b) whether the
last entry + its base reaches the end of the file, and (c) whether the offsets point
into the 27,338-byte tail. If yes, the FNT0 body layout is closed.

### 18.1133 FNT0 OFFSET TABLE: 19 INCREASING ABSOLUTE OFFSETS (0x346..0x392)

1) MEASURED (font_staff.fnt)
```
u32 LE table at 0x346 : 19 entries, strictly increasing, ends at 0x392
first five            : 1074, 2329, 3580, 5246, 7095
last three            : 24262, 25596, 27320
all values < file size (28,176)
last offset           : 27,320  -> distance to EOF = 856 bytes
remaining after table : 27,262 bytes
```
2) INTERPRETATION
```
the values are absolute file offsets into the bitmap/record payload region; 19 entries
means 19 records (not 44 glyphs), so the glyph bitmaps are grouped into 19 blocks
(e.g. pages or sheets) whose sizes are the differences between consecutive offsets.
gaps: 1255, 1251, 1666, 1849, ... (varying block sizes)
```
3) THE FNT0 MAP (final layout so far)
```
0x000..0x01C  header (LE, version 1, tile 32x32)
0x01C..0x12E  sentinel prefix (121 u16)
0x13A..0x242  glyph table: 44 x 6-byte [0][width][code], codes 2..45
0x242..0x346  u16 table: 130 small values (<256)
0x346..0x392  offset table: 19 u32 absolute offsets (last -> 856 bytes before EOF)
...           payload: bitmap blocks addressed by the offset table
```
4) NEXT
```
read the first offset (1074) from the file start and inspect the bytes there: if the
payload begins with a small bitmap header (width/height/format), the FNT0 layout is
closed; compare the 19 block sizes with the glyph counts to see the grouping rule.

as u32 LE: 93635, 94977, 96415, 97721, 98629, 100049, 101670, 103254

### 18.1135 FNT0 CROSS-FILE: font_p5 AND c_font_p5 SHARE IDENTICAL DATA AT 1074

1) THE MEASUREMENT
```
font_staff.fnt  (28,176)   u32 at 1074: 93635, 94977, 96415, 97721
font_p5.fnt   (1,245,122) u32 at 1074: 45, 3014867, 13762560, 47
c_font_p5.fnt (1,167,652) u32 at 1074: 45, 3014867, 13762560, 47   IDENTICAL to p5
header fields  +0x10 / +0x14 / +0x1A:
  staff   : 24 / 274 / 2
  p5      : 24 / 772 / 2
  c_font_p5: 24 / 772 / 2
```
2) INTERPRETATION
```
- font_p5 and c_font_p5 share the SAME content at offset 1074 (four identical u32),
  even though their sizes differ by ~78 KB. So offset 1074 in those two lands inside a
  region with identical structure (same table layout), not inside per-file bitmap data.
- staff's content there is completely different, consistent with it being a much
  smaller font with a different table layout.
- +0x10 = 24 in ALL three files; +0x1A = 2 in ALL three; +0x14 = 274 (staff) vs 772
  (the two p5 fonts) => +0x14 is a per-font parameter, NOT a constant.
```
3) WHAT THIS SETTLES
```
the header field +0x14 varies per font (so it is likely a count or table offset);
+0x10 and +0x1A are constant across the corpus so far.
```
4) NEXT
```
for the p5 pair, dump the region around 1074 (0x400..0x500) and see whether it is a
table of u32 ids (the value 45 looks like a small id). Then check whether 3014867 /
13762560 are offsets in the LARGER file space (both exceed 1.1 MB? no: 3,014,867 >
1,245,122 and 13,762,560 too) => likely ids/hashes again.

### 18.1136 FNT0 HANDOFF (state after section 18.1135)

1) ESTABLISHED (all verified by byte measurement)
```
- FNT0 is LITTLE-ENDIAN (unlike the big-endian GFS0 family)          18.1125
- header: "FNT0", +0x06 version=1, +0x08/+0x0A tile 32x32,

          +0x1A=2 (constant)                                          18.1125/18.1135

(b) grouping rule linking 19 blocks to 44 glyphs;
(c) header fields +0x10 (24) / +0x14 (274/772) / +0x1A (2) meanings;

```
FNT0 was decoded by: endianness test with plausibility constraints (18.1125), longest
sentinel run to pin table start (18.1127), discovering the 6-byte stride from the

the shared prefix is a reliable sample: decoding it once gives the layout for both
fonts. The differing tail is where the per-font bitmap data lives.
```
4) NEXT
```
find the first differing byte between font_p5 and c_font_p5; everything before it is
the shared header/table region and everything after is per-font payload. That single
offset splits FNT0 into "shared tables" and "atlas data" and is the key to closing the
format.

### 18.1139 FNT0: font_p5 vs c_font_p5 FIRST DIFFERENCE IS AT +0x0E (header field)

1) THE DIFF
```

c_font_p5 @0x0E..0x0F : 31 6C   (= 12,652 when read big-endian at +0x0C)
the two files are IDENTICAL from 0x10 onward through at least 0x500 (18.1138)

```
the p5 pair does not diverge at a table boundary - it diverges inside the HEADER:
a font-specific parameter lives at +0x0E (2 bytes, value 0 vs 0x316C-bytes).
everything after it (glyph tables, 0x400..0x500 region) is shared.
=> +0x0E is a per-font parameter, like +0x14 (274 vs 772, 18.1135).
```
3) WHY THIS IS IMPORTANT
```
the shared-table hypothesis (18.1138) is CONFIRMED and localized: the tables really
are common, and the per-font differences are confined to header parameters, with the
payload varying later (files differ in size by ~78 KB).
```

find the first differing byte AFTER 0x500 (scan from 0x500 onward) to locate where the
per-font payload begins; that offset ends the shared-table region.

### 18.1144 FNT0 ARITHMETIC: THE GLYPH BITMAP BLOCK IS THE LAST 22,528 BYTES

1) THE ARITHMETIC (font_staff.fnt, size 28,176)
```
44 glyphs x 32x32 x 4bpp = 44 x 512 = 22,528 bytes
28,176 - 22,528 = 5,648 = 0x1610
=> if the bitmap block is contiguous and ends at EOF, it spans [0x1610, EOF)
   which is EXACTLY 22,528 bytes.
```
2) RESULTING LAYOUT HYPOTHESIS
```
0x000..0x92B  shared tables (header + glyph table + u16 table + 19-entry table)
0x92C..0x1610 intermediate region (3,300 bytes) - still unknown
0x1610..EOF   glyph bitmap block, 22,528 bytes = 44 x (32x32 4bpp)
```
3) WHY THE ARITHMETIC IS COMPELLING
```
the residual after removing a 4bpp 44-glyph atlas is EXACTLY the size of the
remaining payload, leaving the clean intermediate size 3,300. Two independent
constraints (EOF alignment + 512-byte glyph size) are satisfied at once.
```
4) WHAT TO VERIFY NEXT
```
check the bytes at 0x1610: a 4bpp atlas typically starts with visible pixel runs
(e.g. 0xFF/0x00 patterns). Also test the alternative alignment [0x92C, 0x92C+22528)
and see which boundary produces cleaner periodicity at 512-byte intervals.

### 18.1147 FNT0 ALIGNMENT: THE TWO HYPOTHESES ARE ARITHMETICALLY SYMMETRIC

1) THE TWO CANDIDATES
```
(A) atlas at 0x1610 : 0x1610 + 44*512 = 0x6E10 = EOF EXACTLY
    leaves the 3,300-byte region 0x92C..0x1610 BEFORE the atlas.
(B) atlas at 0x92C  : 0x92C + 44*512 = 0x612C, leaving 0x612C..0x6E10 = 3,300 bytes
    AFTER the atlas.
```
2) THE SYMMETRY
```
both candidates use the same 3,300-byte region, only its position differs (before or
after the atlas). The FF-density test (18.1146) returned the same score (27/44) for
both. Therefore neither pure arithmetic nor FF density can decide the alignment.
```
3) WHAT CAN DECIDE IT
```
(a) code side: the eboot font loader (if present) would read the offset to the atlas;
(b) a second font with a DIFFERENT glyph count: the residual region should scale with
    the glyph count in only one of the two interpretations;
(c) row periodicity: 4bpp 32-wide rows are 16 bytes, so a real atlas shows a 16-byte
    periodic pattern when rows are uniform - can be checked with autocorrelation.
```
4) STATUS
```
the glyph-table, shared-region and payload facts (18.1125..18.1145) remain valid;
only the exact atlas start (0x92C vs 0x1610) is open.

### 18.1148 FNT0 ROW-PERIODICITY TEST (16-byte rows) - RESULT

```
4bpp 32-wide glyph rows are 16 bytes; a real atlas whose rows share blank margins shows
higher 16-byte self-similarity than an arbitrary region. The candidate with the higher
percentage is the better atlas start.

### 18.1149 CORRECTION: 0x92C IS NOT A GLOBAL TABLE/PAYLOAD BOUNDARY

1) THE OBSERVATION
```
font_staff @0x92C : FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF 7F 95 18 CC ...  (bitmap-like)
font_p5    @0x92C : 01 01 B5 00 91 00 02 01 B3 00 ...        (table-like u16 values)
=> the same offset holds DIFFERENT KINDS of data in the two fonts.
```
2) THE CORRECTION
```
0x92C is only the point where font_p5 and c_font_p5 diverge (18.1140); it is NOT a
global boundary between shared tables and glyph payload. The shared-region length is
FONT-DEPENDENT (it grows with the number of glyphs / table entries).
=> the file map of 18.1140 must carry this caveat for font_staff.
```
3) WHY THIS RESOLVES THE ALIGNMENT PUZZLE
```
the earlier confusion (0x92C vs 0x1610 as the staff atlas start) came from applying a
p5-specific boundary to the small staff font. For staff, the bitmap payload starts much
earlier than 0x92C; its own atlas start must be derived from its own tables.
```

(130 values) and the 19-entry table, then advance past those structures; the first
bitmap-like bytes after that point are the staff atlas start.

### 18.1154 FNT0 EXACT ARITHMETIC: 44 GLYPHS x 604 BYTES = 26,576 = EOF - 0x640

1) THE HIT
```
file size        : 28,176
EOF - 0x640      : 28,176 - 1,600 = 26,576
44 glyphs x 604  : 26,576        EXACT
604 = 512 (32x32 4bpp bitmap) + 92 (per-glyph extra bytes)
=> atlas candidate: start 0x640, stride 604, 44 glyphs, ends EXACTLY at EOF.
```
2) WHY 604
```
512 bytes is the natural 32x32 4bpp tile; 92 bytes per glyph must hold the per-glyph
metrics not covered by the 6-byte glyph table entry (e.g. bitmap coordinates in the
atlas, row stride, offsets). This is the first decomposition that lands EXACTLY on EOF
with an integer per-glyph size.
```
3) RELATION TO THE EARLIER 0x642
```
the 0x642 reading was two bytes into the candidate atlas (the table terminator scan
ended at 0x642 while the arithmetic boundary is 0x640). This needs one confirmation:
inspect 0x640 vs 0x642 to see which byte is the first atlas byte.
```

### 18.1156 *** FNT0 LAYOUT CLOSED: 92-BYTE GLYPH HEADER + 512-BYTE 4bpp BITMAP ***

1) THE DECISIVE STATISTICS (font_staff.fnt, base 0x640, stride 604)
```

```

0x13A..0x242  glyph table : 44 x 6 bytes [0][width][code], codes 2..45

0x346..0x392  19-entry increasing u32 table
0x392..0x640  172-entry increasing u32 table terminated by 0xFFFFFFFF

```
a native PC renderer can now:

The remaining per-glyph detail is the internal breakdown of the 92-byte header.
```

   0x32C..0xF20][remaining structures][atlas]

### 18.1177 0x812B13B0 IS A PLT IMPORT SLOT (renderList calls go to imports)

ANTI-FORGETTING ENTRY. Keywords: PLT, import slot, 0x812B13B0, 0x812B1400.

1) DISASSEMBLED PATTERN (measured)
```
0x812B13B0  movs r0, r0        ; padding
0x812B13B2  b    #0x812B1B76   ; slot target
0x812B13B8  movs r0, r0
0x812B13BA  b    #0x812B16FE
...
0x812B1400  movs r0, r0
0x812B1402  b    #0x812B1BC6
0x812B1408  movs r0, r0
0x812B140A  b    #0x812B174E
```
2) INTERPRETATION
```
the 8-byte groups of the shape "movs r0,r0 ; b <target>" are PLT (procedure linkage
table) import slots. Therefore the calls seen in renderList (0x812B12E0, 0x812B13B0,
0x812B1400, 0x812B1560, 0x812B1770) are calls to IMPORTED functions, not to engine
functions defined in this eboot.
```
3) CONSEQUENCE
```
to identify what these uploads do we must resolve the import table (NID/name mapping
of this eboot's dynamic imports), then map each PLT slot to its imported symbol.
The PLT targets (0x812B1B76 etc.) are the resolver-side entries.
```
4) NEXT
```
locate the import descriptor / NID table in the eboot (usually a section listing
NID + module + name) and resolve the import behind 0x812B13B0; that names the upload
primitive used by renderList.

### 18.1202 REFINED HYPOTHESIS: off1 INDEXES THE VA-POINTER TABLE REGION, off2 IS THE TARGET

```

(18.1191: 12-byte records whose third field is a code VA).

3) THE RESULTING RECORD READING (hypothesis)
```
record { tag, va_table_off, target_off } describes a PATCH DESCRIPTOR:
  - tag selects the descriptor kind,
  - va_table_off locates a VA slot in the pointer table,
  - target_off is the code position the slot must be fixed up to.
This is consistent with all measured facts: both fields are valid file offsets, off1
clusters in the VA-table region, off2 spreads over code, and there is no in-place value
match at the target (the write goes through the pointer table, not the code).
Rejected alternatives: in-place patch (18.1194), direct branch (18.1198/1199),
function-entry list (18.1199).
```

### 18.1214 TOOLING NOTE: PC-LITERAL DECODE NEEDS capstone detail=True (0-result is a bug)

ANTI-FORGETTING ENTRY. Keywords: capstone detail, literal decode bug, 7 loads.

1) WHAT HAPPENED
```
18.1212 counted 7 pc-relative literal loads in the danceScene routine by matching the
"ldr" mnemonic and "[pc" in the operand text.
18.1213 then tried to resolve the literal ADDRESSES via ins.operands[1].mem.disp and
reported 0 loads - because the Capstone instance was created WITHOUT detail=True, so
operand access raised and every sample was silently skipped.
=> the 18.1213 zero count is a TOOLING BUG, not a measurement. The 7 loads stand.
```
2) THE FIX (for the next round)
```
md = Cs(CS_ARCH_ARM, CS_MODE_THUMB); md.detail = True
then use:
  op = ins.operands[1]  # CS_OP_MEM
  imm = op.mem.disp
Thumb literal address = ((ins.address + 4) & ~3) + imm
file offset = 0x10E0 + (literal_va - 0x81000000)
```
3) STATUS
```
danceScene 0x8100993C..0x81009CF0: 334 instructions, 0 direct bl/blx,
7 pc-literal loads (addresses still UNDECODED due to the bug above).

### 18.1216 *** DECISIVE: ALL 7 LITERALS ARE 0x66666667 = ARM SIGNED DIVIDE-BY-10 CONSTANT ***

```
2) THE SEMANTICS (compiler constant)
```
0x66666667 is the ARM magic multiplier for SIGNED INTEGER DIVISION BY 10
(the sequence is typically: smull / add / asr to compute x/10).
=> this dance-scene routine performs repeated integer divisions by 10, i.e. DIGIT
   EXTRACTION / decimal formatting (score, time, frame counters) - not geometry math.
```

The literal pools (0x81009C28 / 0x81009CAC / 0x81009CEC) are inside the function body.
```

### 18.1218 CORRECTION: 0x66666667 WITH asr #1 IS DIVIDE-BY-5 (not /10); 0xAAAAAAAB IS /3

ANTI-FORGETTING ENTRY. Keywords: divide by 5, divide by 3, 0xAAAAAAAB, rounding +4.

1) THE EXACT SEQUENCE (measured)
```
0x81009B96 ldr   r1, [pc, #0x90]      ; r1 = 0x66666667
0x81009B98 adds  r0, #4               ; rounding: x + 4
0x81009B9A smull r2, r1, r1, r0       ; 64-bit product
0x81009B9E asrs  r0, r0, #0x1f        ; sign(x)
0x81009BA0 rsb   r0, r0, r1, asr #1   ; (hi >> 1) - sign  => total shift 33
```
2) THE ARITHMETIC
```
0x66666667 = 1717986919 ~= 2^33 / 5 = 1717986918.4
=> the sequence computes (x + 4) / 5 (rounded), NOT x / 10.
THEREFORE the 18.1216 claim "signed divide by 10" is RETRACTED: it is DIVIDE BY 5.
A second constant appears at 0x81009BAA: movs.w r1, #-0x55555556 = 0xAAAAAAAB
  0xAAAAAAAB = 2863311531 ~= 2^33 / 3  => DIVIDE BY 3.
```
3) WHAT THE FUNCTION DOES (revised)
```
the routine performs small-integer divisions by 5 and by 3 (with rounding), i.e. unit
or base conversions / decimal-ish formatting of one or more counters. Not geometry.
```
4) NEXT
```
enumerate all magic constants inside this routine and map each to its divisor; then
identify the struct fields (r5+offset) feeding each division.

### 18.1227 *** CORRECTION: THE SIX "GLOBAL WRITES" ARE LITERAL-POOL BYTES *** 

ANTI-FORGETTING ENTRY. Keywords: literal pool misread, linear sweep, 0x66666667 as code.

1) THE PROOF
```
the decoded literal pool address is 0x81009C28 (from 18.1215) and it holds the bytes
67 66 66 66 = 0x66666667 (the divide-by-5 magic).
Thumb-encoded, the 16-bit word 0x6667 decodes as  "str r7, [r4, #0x64]" :
   0110 0 11001 100 111  -> STR imm5=25, Rn=4, Rt=7
=> the "six writes to [r4,#0x64]" found by the linear sweep (18.1225/18.1226) are the
   SAME literal-pool bytes being misinterpreted as instructions. THEY ARE NOT CODE.
   Both sections' write claim is RETRACTED.
```
2) WHY IT HAPPENED
```
the disassembly swept linearly from the function entry without following control flow,
so inline literal pools (placed inside the function body) were decoded as instructions.
The 334-instruction count therefore INCLUDES pool bytes; the real code size is smaller.
```
3) WHAT STILL STANDS
```
- function entry 0x8100993C with push.w {...lr} and stack frame 0x2F8
- parameter struct byte fields at +0x04,+0x05,+0x07,+0x08,+0x09,+0x0A,+0x0B,+0x0C
  (these came from regex over operand text but also may include pool artifacts - to be
   re-verified with flow-following disassembly)
- literals 0x81009C28 / 0x81009CAC / 0x81009CEC = 0x66666667 (divide by 5)
- 0xAAAAAAAB divide-by-3 immediate at 0x81009BAA (an instruction, not a pool)
```
4) NEXT (method fix)
```
disassemble with CONTROL-FLOW FOLLOWING: start at 0x8100993C, follow branches, and when
a branch targets the instruction after an unconditional b/ bx lr, treat the skipped gap
as a literal pool. Only then count field accesses and writes.

### 18.1244 *** ROOT CAUSE FOUND: CAPSTONE RETURNS SIGNED 32-BIT IMMEDIATES ***

ANTI-FORGETTING ENTRY. Keywords: signed immediate, 0x80000000, mask fix, negative targets.

1) THE BUG
```
Capstone returns CS_OP_IMM values as SIGNED 32-bit integers. For any VA >= 0x80000000
the value becomes negative on this ARM/Vita image:
  op_str says  #0x811EA3E6
  operands[0].imm equals  -0x7EE15C1A   ( = 0x811EA3E6 - 2^32 )
```
2) THE FIX (applied to tools/trace_func.py)
```
correct = imm & 0xFFFFFFFF
```
3) WHAT THIS FIXES
```
(a) 18.1242's "all-negative bl targets" were NOT misdecoded instructions: they were
    correct targets with the sign extension artefact. The earlier conclusion that the
    linear sweep is unreliable is therefore WRONG for that reason (the sweep may still
    have other issues, but negative targets are explained by this bug).
(b) the reliable call-graph path is now open: run trace_func with the mask fix.
```
4) TOOL
```
py -3 tools\trace_func.py 811E7C6C --calls

```
void renderList(void* arg0) {
    stack frame 0x34, stack guard 0x812B414C;
    sub_811EA3E6(arg0);                       // first: call the big inner routine
    Global* g = (Global*)0x816CBC08;
    if ((s8)g->b_5CC) {                       // flag at +0x5CC
        if ((s8)g->b_918)  SceGxm_12AAA7AF(&g->d_9B0, 0);
        else               SceGxm_12AAA7AF(&g->d_15C, 0);
    }
    ...
}
```
2) CONFIRMED CONSTANTS / OFFSETS
```
BSS base            0x816CBC08
flag byte           +0x5CC   (ldrsb, conditional)
flag byte           +0x918   (ldrsb, conditional)
struct pointer      +0x9B0   (arg0 of first SceGxm call in one branch)
struct pointer      +0x15C   (arg0 in the other branch)
call ABI            r0 = struct pointer, r1 = 0
first SceGxm NID    0x12AAA7AF (PLT 0x812B1250)
inner callee        0x811EA3E6 (called with the same arg0)
```
3) WHY IT MATTERS
```
this is the first render-layer routine expressed as runnable pseudo-code with real
globals, flags and call ABI - the level of detail the native port needs. Continue the
same per-call decode for the remaining 57 SceGxm calls.

### 18.1312 *** CORRECTION: 0x811E6A4C IS A 3-INSTRUCTION FORWARDER; trace_func HAD A RETURN-STOP BUG ***

ANTI-FORGETTING ENTRY. Keywords: 0x811E6A4C 3 instructions, pop pc terminal, trace bug.

1) THE CORRECTION (supersedes the body description in 18.1310)
```
0x811E6A4C push {r4,lr} ; blx 0x812B2270 ; pop {r4,pc}      -> 3 instructions, 1 call
0x811E6A54 push {r4,lr} ; blx 0x812B2350 ; pop {r4,pc}      -> SEPARATE function
0x811E6A5C push {r4,lr} ; blx 0x812B2290 ; pop {r4,pc}      -> SEPARATE function
=> 0x811E6A4C is a 3-instruction forwarder to SceLibc func_nid 0x7205BFDB (PLT 0x812B2270).
   The earlier "10 instructions / 3 calls / one shared helper" reading was WRONG: the
   tracer continued past the function return into the next two 3-instr functions.
```
2) TOOL BUG AND FIX (tools/trace_func.py)
```
bug : traversal only stopped at 'bx'; 'pop {...,pc}' (function return) was not terminal,
      so paths ran into subsequent functions and inflated instruction/call counts.
fix : stop when an instruction writes pc: pop {...pc}, ldr pc,...,
      mov/add/sub pc,...
```
3) CONSEQUENCE
```
counts for any function ending in 'pop {..pc}' were OVERESTIMATED. Functions already
analysed must be re-traced to confirm their counts; renderList (0x811E7C6C) and the
wrappers are re-measured with the fixed tool in this round (see appended tool output).
The structural findings about data offsets/constants remain valid (they were read from
actual instructions), but instruction/call COUNTS from earlier sections are upper bounds.

stack[0] = 0 ; stack[4] = a4 ; stack[8] = a5 ; stack[0xC] = a6
r = SceGxm_PLT_0x812B1470(a1, a2, a3, 0, stack)     // blx 0x812B1470
return (r == 0) ? 1 : 0
```

void sub_811EF596(void* a0, u32* flags) {
    const u8* base = (const u8*)0x81513EB8;   // tables: B at +4, A at +8, stride 0x48
    for (int i = 0; i < 15; i++) {
        if (flags[i] != 0) {
            SceGxm_65DD0C84(a0, flags[i], 0,
                            *(u32*)(base + 4 + i*0x48),
                            (u32*)(base + 8 + i*0x48));
        }
    }
}
```

table B         base+4, stride 0x48, element read as u32
table A         base+8, stride 0x48, element passed as pointer

input array a1  u32 entries, stride 4
```

### 18.1347 *** MATERIAL-UPLOAD ROUTINE COMPLETE: 34 ITERATIONS AT 0x811EFE24 ***

ANTI-FORGETTING ENTRY. Keywords: 0x811EFE24, 34 entries, material table full size.

1) EXACT BODY (22 instructions, ends 0x811EFE66)
```
0x811EFE24 push.w {r4,r5,r6,r7,r8,lr} ; sub sp,#8
0x811EFE2A r2 = 0x815142F0                       ; MATERIAL TABLE base
0x811EFE32 r4 = a1                               ; flags array
0x811EFE34 r6 = a0                               ; context
0x811EFE36 r7 = r2 + 8 ; 0x811EFE3A r5 = r2 + 4
0x811EFE3C r8 = 0                                ; i
LOOP:
0x811EFE40 r1 = *r4                              ; flag = flags[i]
0x811EFE42 cbnz r1, DO_CALL
0x811EFE44 r8++ ; r4 += 4 ; r5 += 0x48 ; r7 += 0x48
0x811EFE4E cmp r8, #0x22                         ; i < 34
0x811EFE52 blo LOOP
0x811EFE54 b DONE
DO_CALL:
0x811EFE56 r3 = *r5 ; r0 = r6 ; [sp] = r7 ; r2 = 0
0x811EFE5E blx 0x812B13B0                        ; SceGxm_65DD0C84(a0, flag, 0, count, ptr)
0x811EFE62 b LOOP
DONE: 0x811EFE64 add sp,#8 ; 0x811EFE66 pop.w {r4,r5,r6,r7,r8,pc}
```
2) IMPLEMENTABLE C
```
void sub_811EFE24(void* a0, u32* flags) {
    const u8* base = (const u8*)0x815142F0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 34; i++)
        if (flags[i])
            SceGxm_65DD0C84(a0, flags[i], 0,
                            *(u32*)(base + 4 + i*0x48),
                            (u32*)(base + 8 + i*0x48));
}
```

(d) material parameters come from material resource data (table of 34 values);
(e) call the upload helper once per entry that has a non-zero flag/handle.
```

2) IMPLEMENTABLE C

void sub_811EF5DC(void* a0, u32 index, const u32* flags) {
    u32 h = flags[index];
    if (!h) return;
    const u8* base = (const u8*)0x81513EB8;
    SceGxm_65DD0C84(a0,
                    h,
                    0,
                    *(u32*)(base + 4 + index*0x48),
                    (void*)(base + 8 + index*0x48));
}

```
this is the single-entry variant of 0x811EF596 (18.1334): the loop version iterates 15
slots; this function uploads ONE slot selected by index. The index*0x48 computation is done
explicitly with shift/add instructions (index*9 then <<3).

### 18.1380 *** EXACT .GSC LAYOUT: GFS0 > GSC0 > PVSG RECORDS > GXP PROGRAMS ***

ANTI-FORGETTING ENTRY. Keywords: GSC exact layout, GXP header, 0x03500501, GSC0.

1) MEASURED BYTES (GFDPSP2.GSC, first 0x60)
```
+0x00: 47 46 53 30  "GFS0"    ; outer container magic
+0x04: 01 10 51 00             ; type word  (0x01105100 family)
+0x08: 00 00 00 04
+0x0C: 00 00 00 00
+0x10: 47 53 43 30  "GSC0"    ; inner shader-collection magic
+0x14: 01 08 71 59             ; collection type word
+0x18: 00 00 00 04
+0x1C: 00 00 00 00
+0x20: 00 00 00 00
+0x24: 02 4C 00 00             ; 0x4C02 (size/count candidate)
+0x28: 00 00 20 02

+0x30: 00 00 00 00

+0x40: 50 56 53 47  "PVSG"    ; FIRST SHADER RECORD magic
+0x44: 44 02 00 00             ; record size = 0x244
+0x48: 47 58 50 00  "GXP\0"   ; shader program magic
+0x4C: 01 05 50 03             ; GXP type word (0x03500501)
+0x50: 44 02 00 00             ; program size = 0x244
+0x54: F1 EB 54 C5
+0x58: 22 F1 C7 FE
+0x5C: 00 00 19 00
```
2) RECORD FORMAT
```
PVSG record  = "PVSG" + u32 record_size + GXP program payload
GXP program  = "GXP\0" + u32 gxp_type + u32 program_size + hashes/fields + code
record count : 340 PVSG occurrences in GFDPSP2.GSC (one per shader program)
```
3) SIGNIFICANCE
```
.GSC files are GFS0-wrapped shader collections; the actual shader binaries are GXP
programs (the PS Vita GXM program container). The native port must parse PVSG records and
map GXP programs onto its GL shader pipeline (translation or replacement).
This connects the 49-uniform contract (18.1350) to the concrete shader assets that consume
those uniforms.
```

2) THE KEY OBSERVATION
```
the FIRST PVSG record spans 0x40..0x284 (record size 0x244), and the first uniform name
appears at 0x270 - i.e. INSIDE the first program, near its tail. Therefore every GXP program
carries its own uniform-name table (its declared interface), not just the global 49-uniform
lists in the eboot data segment.
```
3) WHY THIS MATTERS
```
the renderer binds uniforms by NAME per program. For the native port this means:
  - each of the 340 programs can be mapped to the exact uniform set it consumes;
  - no guessing which of the 49 uniforms a given material shader needs;
  - the name tables can be extracted program-by-program and used to generate GLSL
    uniform declarations per shader variant.
```

### 18.1394 *** PROGRAMS DECLARE STAGE + ATTRIBUTES + UNIFORMS; +0x2C = TOTAL DECLARED NAMES ***

ANTI-FORGETTING ENTRY. Keywords: vertex position color texcoord0 declarations, count +0x2C verified.

1) THE DISCOVERED DECLARATION STRINGS (measured per program)
```
prog@0x40    size 0x244  count(+0x2C)=3
   strings: "PVSGD", "GXP", "vertex", "position", "mtxLocalToWorld", "mtxV..."
prog@0xB5C   size 0x264  count=4
   strings: "PVSGd", "GXP", "vertex", "position", "vertex", "color",
            "mtxLocalToWorld", "mtxView..."

   strings: "vertex", "position", "vertex", "color", "vertex", "texcoord0",
            "mtxLocalToWorld", "mtxVie..."
prog@0x25A4  size 0x268  count=4
   strings: "vertex", "position", "vertex", "texcoord0", "mtxLocalToWorld", "mtxView..."
```
2) THE COUNT RELATION (verified on all four samples)
```
+0x2C = number of DECLARED NAMES = (# attributes) + (# uniforms)
  prog@0x40  : 1 attr (position)              + 2 uniforms = 3  = count
  prog@0xB5C : 2 attr (position, color)       + 2 uniforms = 4  = count
  prog@0x1730: 3 attr (position,color,texcoord0) + 2 uniforms = 5 = count
  prog@0x25A4: 2 attr (position, texcoord0)   + 2 uniforms = 4  = count
=> the +0x2C field is confirmed as the declared-name count.
```
3) DECLARATION VOCABULARY SEEN SO FAR
```
stages     : "vertex" (fragment presumably appears in other programs)
attributes : "position", "color", "texcoord0" (texcoord1/2 likely follow the UV uniform set)
uniforms   : "mtxLocalToWorld", "mtxViewProj", ... (the 49-uniform contract names)
```
4) SIGNIFICANCE
```

  @0x33D4 size=0x1A0 count=4 predicted 0x264
  @0x41AC size=0x1C0 count=5 predicted 0x284
  @0x5060 size=0x154 count=3 predicted 0x244
  @0x51DC size=0x150 count=3 predicted 0x244
=> THE FORMULA OF 18.1405 IS RETRACTED. It was a three-sample coincidence.
```
